title: The Gibeonites (Joshua 9)
hook: tricked into a treaty, Israel keeps its oath anyway

segments.voice: Yesterday, Achan, and what he buried in his tent. Your line was one hidden thing affects all. Today, a trick, and a promise.

Dry bread, gone moldy and crumbling. Wineskins split and tied back together. Sandals patched and worn through. Clothes worn old. A group of strangers walks into Israel's camp at Gilgal carrying all of it like evidence. We've come from a very far country, they say. Look at our bread: it was warm from the oven the day we left. Make a treaty with us. They are lying. They live just over the hills, in Gibeon, and they've heard what happened at Jericho and Ai. The costume is the whole plan.
screen: `MOLDY BREAD, WORN SANDALS.` → `A VERY FAR COUNTRY.` → `THE COSTUME IS THE PLAN.`

segments.voice: And it works. The men of Israel look at the bread, taste it, and take it as proof. The text stops to point out what they skip: they didn't ask counsel of the Lord. Joshua makes peace with them, and the leaders of the congregation swear an oath to let them live. A few days later the truth comes out. The far country is next door. The people are furious, and grumble against their leaders. And the leaders say the sentence the chapter turns on: we have sworn to them by the Lord, the God of Israel, so we may not touch them. The oath was gotten by a lie. It still holds. The Gibeonites are spared, and they become, in the text's phrase, "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the people and for the altar. Did the oath bind as a valid contract? Some rabbis in the Talmud say no: it was made under false pretenses, but breaking it would have disgraced God's name before the nations. Either way, the promise outlives everyone in the room. Much later, the book of Samuel tells of a famine in King David's day, and traces it back to Saul, who had attacked the Gibeonites though Israel had sworn to them. The oath at Gilgal still bound. A psalm describes the person who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and one line fits this chapter exactly: "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."
screen: `THEY DIDN'T ASK.` · `WE HAVE SWORN: WE MAY NOT TOUCH THEM.` · `GOD'S NAME, NOT A CONTRACT.` · `STILL BINDING IN DAVID'S DAY.` · then, large: `SWEARETH TO HIS OWN HURT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise that has become inconvenient: made too fast, or the situation changed, or, like Israel's leaders, you'd have said no if you'd known more. Don't decide yet whether you're bound; just picture keeping it, the actual hour, the actual phone call, and notice what it costs and what it would say about your word. If you pray, hold the psalm's line: he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
The Gibeonites. The neighbors who tricked Israel into a treaty, and were protected by the oath anyway. Today's word.
Your line: an oath is kept. Even one gotten by a trick. Day seven hundred four.

howItsDone: In Jewish law vows and oaths are binding; the Kol Nidrei service on the eve of Yom Kippur addresses vows, and some Jews say bli neder, "without a vow", when promising something, to avoid an unintended oath.

chat.says: If the Gibeonites lied to get the treaty, why did Israel still keep it?
options: They'd sworn by God's name; breaking it would disgrace that name.
The treaty was fair, since Gibeon really was a very far country.
They kept it only until Joshua died, and then it no longer held.
chat.meaning: The leaders say: we have sworn by the Lord, so we may not touch them. Some rabbis add that breaking it would disgrace God's name.
